subject: Polity
topic: Election Commission of India III — mixed tiers
description: Article 324, CEC + EC composition, removal, MCC, EVM-VVPAT, recent reforms

questions.stem: The Election Commission of India is a constitutional body created by which Article?

options.option_text: Article 280, providing for the Finance Commission
Article 324, providing for the Election Commission
Article 148, dealing with the Comptroller & Auditor General
Article 76, dealing with the Attorney General of India

questions.explanation: Article 324 — Election Commission of India (ECI). Established 25 January 1950 (the day before India became a republic). National Voters' Day celebrated annually on 25 Jan. Independent constitutional body. Conducts elections to Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies + Councils, Office of President + Vice-President. State elections (panchayats, municipalities) are the State Election Commissions' job under Articles 243K and 243ZA — separate bodies, not ECI.

questions.stem: The current composition of the Election Commission of India is:

options.option_text: Single CEC alone, as originally a one-member body
Multi-member: CEC + 2 Election Commissioners (since 1993)
Five Election Commissioners decided by ruling party
Three Election Commissioners chosen by Supreme Court alone

questions.explanation: ECI history: Originally 1-member body (CEC only) from 1950. Briefly 3-member in 1989-90, then back to 1-member, then PERMANENTLY made 3-member from 1 October 1993 (CEC + 2 ECs). Each has equal voting power; majority decision when there's disagreement. ECs are appointed by the President. Recently — Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 specifies a selection committee (PM + LoP + Cabinet Minister; replaced an earlier proposed CJI inclusion that the SC had directed in Anoop Baranwal 2023 case).

questions.stem: The CHIEF ELECTION COMMISSIONER (CEC) can be REMOVED FROM OFFICE:

options.option_text: By the President alone at his sole discretion at any time
Only by the procedure used to remove a Supreme Court judge
By the Prime Minister together with cabinet approval
By a vote of two-thirds of the ruling party in Parliament

questions.explanation: Article 324(5) — CEC can be removed only via the SAME procedure as a Supreme Court Judge — i.e., by IMPEACHMENT: requires majority of total membership of EACH House of Parliament + 2/3 of those present and voting. Grounds: PROVED MISBEHAVIOUR or INCAPACITY. Strong protection ensures independence. ELECTION COMMISSIONERS (other than CEC) — can be removed only on the recommendation of the CEC (a weaker protection). Distractor 1 wrongly gives President discretion. Distractors 3, 4 wrongly involve cabinet / ruling-party power.

questions.stem: The MODEL CODE OF CONDUCT (MCC) of the ECI:

options.option_text: Is a statutory legal code with defined penal provisions
Is a non-statutory set of guidelines binding by political consensus
Comes into force only on polling day every election cycle
Applies only to the ruling party in the central government

questions.explanation: MCC — set of NON-STATUTORY norms first issued by ECI in 1968 (Kerala assembly elections). Now a comprehensive document on what political parties + candidates can/cannot do during elections. ENFORCEABILITY — political consensus + ECI persuasion + 'naming and shaming'. NOT legally binding (proposals to give it statutory force have been debated). KICKS IN: from the date of election announcement, until results declared. Applies to ALL parties + candidates (ruling + opposition). Recent additions: bans on misuse of social media, deep-fakes, AI-generated content (post-2024 election rules).

questions.stem: VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail) was introduced in Indian elections to:

options.option_text: Replace the EVM completely with paper ballots once again
Provide a paper-slip record verifying each EVM vote cast
Speed up the counting of votes after polling concludes
Allow voting from home through a paper postal ballot

questions.explanation: VVPAT — paper slip showing the candidate name + symbol of the chosen vote, visible behind a glass for ~7 seconds, then deposited in a sealed box. Allows post-election verification — EC mandated since 2019, slips from 5 randomly chosen polling stations per assembly constituency are matched against EVM count. Reasoning: address allegations about EVM tampering. SC (Apr 2024) — declined 100% VVPAT verification but kept the 5/constituency rule. Distractor 1 — VVPAT supplements EVM, doesn't replace. Distractor 3 — actually adds time. Distractor 4 — different mechanism (postal ballot for absentee voting).

questions.stem: The first Chief Election Commissioner of India was:

options.option_text: T.N. Seshan, the famous reformist CEC of the early 1990s
Sukumar Sen, who oversaw the first general election in 1951-52
M.S. Gill, who later became a Union Cabinet Minister
James Michael Lyngdoh, of the Bihar 2005 election fame

questions.explanation: Sukumar Sen (ICS officer) — FIRST CEC of India, 1950-1958. Conducted the FIRST GENERAL ELECTIONS (1951-52) — a logistical marvel: 173 million eligible voters, only 15% literate, 224,000 polling booths, 2 million ballot boxes, ~16,500 candidates for 489 LS seats. He pioneered the use of separate ballot boxes and party symbols (necessary for illiterate voters). T.N. SESHAN (CEC 1990-96) — 10th CEC, transformed the office: introduced voter ID cards, enforced MCC strictly. Lyngdoh (2001-04) — known for free + fair Bihar 2005 polls.

questions.stem: NOTA (None Of The Above) was introduced as a voting option in Indian general elections starting from:

options.option_text: 2009 Lok Sabha elections, on initial Supreme Court suggestion
2013 state elections, after Supreme Court order in PUCL v. Union of India
2019 Lok Sabha elections, with new EVM design changes
2024 elections, as part of pandemic-era voting reforms

questions.explanation: NOTA — introduced 2013 (Sept 2013 SC ruling in PUCL v. Union of India). First used in November 2013 state elections (Chhattisgarh, MP, Rajasthan, Mizoram, Delhi). Allows voters to formally REJECT all candidates without spoiling the ballot. SYMBOL — a stylised ballot paper with a black cross. NOTA votes don't elect anyone (highest non-NOTA vote-getter wins) — essentially a 'protest' vote. Recently the SC reaffirmed (2024) that NOTA majority doesn't trigger re-election in single-candidate constituencies, though the ECI introduced 're-election' if NOTA wins, in some specific conditions.
